title: 03. Databases & Data Modeling: Replication
summary: Replication is the practice of copying data from a primary database node to one or more replica nodes, so that the system survives node failures, scales read throughput, and can place data geographically close to users — at…

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Replication is the practice of copying data from a **primary** database node to one or more **replica** nodes, so that the system survives node failures, scales read throughput, and can place data geographically close to users — at the cost of consistency trade-offs (synchronous vs asynchronous) and write-amplification overhead.

Replication is the foundation of every durable, available database system. A single-node database is one disk failure away from data loss and one network blip away from unavailability. Replication solves both: with N copies of the data on N machines, the system tolerates N-1 failures transparently, and read throughput scales roughly linearly with replica count. The trade-off is **consistency vs latency vs availability** — the three poles of the CAP theorem. Synchronous replication gives strong consistency (a committed write is guaranteed to be on the replicas) but adds write latency (wait for replicas to ack) and reduces availability (if a replica is down, the write fails). Asynchronous replication gives low latency and high availability (the primary commits and returns immediately; replicas catch up later) but introduces **replication lag** — a window during which the replicas are stale. The choice depends on the workload: financial transactions demand synchronous replication; a social media feed tolerates asynchronous replication with seconds of lag.

The three replication topologies are **single-leader**, **multi-leader**, and **leaderless**. **Single-leader** (also called primary-secondary, master-slave) designates one node as the primary — all writes go to it, and replicas apply the stream of changes. Reads can go to the primary or to replicas. This is the most common topology because it preserves a single sequential order of writes (no conflicts). The trade-off: the primary is a write bottleneck and a single point of failure for writes; if it goes down, a failover promotes a replica (typically 10-60 seconds). **Multi-leader** allows multiple nodes to accept writes, with bidirectional replication between them. Useful for multi-region deployments where users in the US write to a US primary and users in EU write to an EU primary — latency stays low for both. The trade-off: write conflicts when both leaders update the same row; resolution requires conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs), last-writer-wins, or application-level merge logic. **Leaderless** (Dynamo-style) allows any node to accept writes and reads; the client writes to N nodes (with a quorum W) and reads from N nodes (with a quorum R), and W+R>N ensures consistency. Cassandra, DynamoDB, and Riak use this. The trade-off: no failover delay (any node can serve any request), but conflict resolution at read time.

The two replication mechanisms are **statement-based** and **log-based** (also called logical and physical). **Statement-based** replication ships the SQL statements (`INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 'Alice')`) and replays them on replicas. Pros: compact log, database-agnostic. Cons: non-deterministic statements (`NOW()`, `RAND()`, auto-increment) produce different results on the replica, breaking consistency. MySQL's original binlog format was statement-based; it's now mostly obsolete. **Log-based / physical replication** ships the binary changes (the WAL — write-ahead log — in PostgreSQL, or the row-based binlog in MySQL). Each log entry represents a low-level change ("row 42 in table users, set column name to 'Alice'"). Pros: deterministic, exact replica of the primary. Cons: log is large; replica must run the same database version. PostgreSQL's streaming replication ships WAL records over a TCP connection — the replica applies them as they arrive, staying within milliseconds of the primary. **Logical replication** (a third option) decodes the WAL into a higher-level stream of changes (insert/update/delete per table), allowing cross-version replication and selective table replication. PostgreSQL's logical replication (added in v10) is used for upgrade migrations and CDC pipelines (Debezium).

Real-world: PostgreSQL streaming replication is the canonical example. A primary writes WAL records to disk (and optionally to a `pg_wal` directory); replicas connect over TCP and stream the WAL as it's generated. With `synchronous_commit=on` and `synchronous_standby_names='replica1'`, the primary waits for replica1 to flush the WAL before acknowledging the commit to the client — strong consistency, ~2x write latency. With `synchronous_commit=off` or no synchronous standbys, the primary commits immediately and the replica catches up asynchronously — write latency is low, but if the primary crashes before the replica receives the WAL, the committed transaction is lost (data loss window of up to a few seconds). The classic HA setup: 1 primary + 1 synchronous replica (zero data loss, automatic failover via Patroni) + N async replicas (for read scaling). Real-world: Amazon RDS PostgreSQL uses this pattern; Netflix runs PostgreSQL with Patroni across multiple AWS Availability Zones.

Real-world: MySQL's binlog replication is older and battle-tested. The primary writes events to a binary log (`binlog`); replicas connect, fetch binlog events via a "dump" thread, and apply them via a "SQL thread" (in older versions) or parallel worker threads (in MySQL 5.7+). The binlog has three formats: STATEMENT (SQL text — fast but non-deterministic), ROW (row changes — large but exact), and MIXED (statement for safe queries, row for non-deterministic). Modern MySQL defaults to ROW. Statement-based replication can break in subtle ways — `INSERT INTO audit SELECT NOW(), user FROM sessions` runs at different times on primary and replica, producing different timestamps. Facebook ran MySQL at scale for years (still does for some workloads) with sophisticated tooling around binlog replication, including "MySQLraft" (a Raft-based consensus layer replacing traditional async replication for stronger consistency).

Real-world: Amazon Aurora reimagines replication by separating compute from storage. The storage layer is a distributed, replicated log across 6 copies (3 AZs × 2 copies) — writes go to a quorum of 4/6, reads from any of 6. The compute layer (the "instance") is stateless and reads pages from the storage layer on demand. This allows Aurora to add up to 15 read replicas sharing the same storage — adding a replica is instant (no data copy) and replicas have zero replication lag (they read the same shared storage). Traditional PostgreSQL/MySQL replicas have their own storage and lag behind the primary; Aurora replicas share storage and stay in sync. The trade-off: Aurora's storage is more expensive (6 copies) and the architecture is proprietary.

The CAP theorem governs replication trade-offs during partitions. When the network between two data centers fails (a partition), you must choose: **CP** (consistency + partition tolerance) — refuse writes to maintain consistency, sacrificing availability; **AP** (availability + partition tolerance) — accept writes on both sides, sacrificing consistency (conflicts to resolve later). Single-leader with synchronous replication is CP — if the replica is unreachable, writes fail. Multi-leader and leaderless are AP — both sides keep accepting writes, with conflict resolution on reconnect. The choice depends on the application: a banking ledger must be CP (no double-spends); a shopping cart can be AP (conflict resolution: highest quantity wins). MongoDB (with WriteConcern=majority) is CP; Cassandra (with consistency level ONE) is AP. Real-world: Netflix uses AP for viewing history (you can watch offline; conflicts resolve to "latest position") but CP for billing.

sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD W["Client write"] --> P["Primary
(accepts writes)"] P -->|"sync: wait for ack"| SR["Sync Replica
(zero data loss)"] P -.->|"async: stream WAL"| AR1["Async Replica 1
(ms-sec lag)"] P -.->|"async: stream WAL"| AR2["Async Replica 2
(ms-sec lag)"] SR --> Ack["Ack to client
(after sync replica confirms)"] Ack --> W R["Client read"] --> Router{Read routing} Router -->|"strong: latest write"| P Router -->|"eventual: stale OK"| AR1 Router -->|"eventual: stale OK"| AR2 P -.->|"failure"| Failover["Failover
promote sync replica"] Failover --> SR ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` SINGLE-LEADER (most common): +----------+ write ---------->| Primary | +----+-----+ | +----------+----------+----------+ | sync (wait) | | v v v +----------+ +----------+ +----------+ |Sync Repl | |Async R1 | |Async R2 | | (zero | | (lag ms) | | (lag ms) | | loss) | +----------+ +----------+ +----------+ | failover target MULTI-LEADER (multi-region): +----------+ +----------+ | US Lead | <-- bidirectional->| EU Lead | +----------+ replicate +----------+ ^ ^ US writes EU writes (low latency) (low latency) conflict resolution on same row -> CRDT / LWW / app merge LEADERLESS (Dynamo-style, Cassandra): Client writes to N nodes (quorum W) Client reads from N nodes (quorum R) W + R > N -> strong consistency W + R <= N -> eventual consistency +---+ +---+ +---+ | A | | B | | C | (replication factor 3) +---+ +---+ +---+ write to A,B (W=2) -> ack read from B,C (R=2) -> B has latest, C stale -> return B ``` ### Walkthrough 1. The client sends a write to the primary. The primary writes the change to its WAL (write-ahead log) and either waits for replicas to confirm (synchronous) or commits immediately and streams the WAL asynchronously. The client receives an ack only after the configured consistency level is met. 2. Replicas receive the WAL stream and apply the changes. A synchronous replica is always caught up to the primary's last commit; an asynchronous replica may lag by milliseconds to seconds depending on network and load. Reads routed to replicas see data as of the replica's last applied WAL position. 3. If the primary fails, a failover detection mechanism (Patroni, Consul, RDS multi-AZ) promotes a synchronous replica to primary. Clients update their connection strings; the new primary accepts writes. Total downtime: typically 10-60 seconds (detection + promotion + client rerouting).

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Mock of sync vs async replication latency.
- Apply WAL up to lsn; returns True if ack received.
- Simulate a write with replication.
- 2. wait for sync replica ack (max RTT of sync replicas)
- Sync replica down -> write fails (CP behavior)
- Async replicas catch up in background
- Async: stream to all replicas in background, return immediately
- Setup: 1 primary + 3 replicas (1 sync + 2 async) -- classic HA

**Defines:** `Replica`, `Primary`, `benchmark()`

```python
"""
Mock of sync vs async replication latency.

Models:
  1. Synchronous replication: primary waits for replica ack before
     returning to client. Latency = max(primary_write, replica_rtt).
  2. Asynchronous replication: primary returns immediately; replica
     catches up later. Latency = primary_write only.

  Shows the latency / durability trade-off with simulated failures.

Run:  python3 replication_demo.py
"""

import time
import random
import threading
from collections import deque

class Replica:
    def __init__(self, name, rtt_ms):
        self.name = name
        self.rtt_ms = rtt_ms              # round-trip time to primary
        self.lag_ms = 0                   # how far behind the primary
        self.alive = True
        self.applied_lsn = 0              # last applied log sequence number

    def apply(self, lsn, primary_lsn):
        """Apply WAL up to `lsn`; returns True if ack received."""
        if not self.alive:
            return False
        time.sleep(self.rtt_ms / 1000.0)  # network + apply delay
        self.applied_lsn = lsn
        self.lag_ms = (primary_lsn - lsn) * 10  # rough lag estimate
        return True

class Primary:
    def __init__(self, name, replicas, sync_mode):
        self.name = name
        self.replicas = replicas
        self.sync_mode = sync_mode       # 'sync' or 'async'
        self.lsn = 0                     # current log sequence number
        self.write_ms = 5                # local write latency

    def write(self, payload):
        """Simulate a write with replication."""
        self.lsn += 1
        t0 = time.time()

        # 1. local write
        time.sleep(self.write_ms / 1000.0)

        if self.sync_mode == 'sync':
            # 2. wait for sync replica ack (max RTT of sync replicas)
            sync_replica = self.replicas[0]   # first replica is sync
            acked = sync_replica.apply(self.lsn, self.lsn)
            if not acked:
                # sync replica down -> write fails (CP behavior)
                return {"ok": False, "latency_ms": (time.time()-t0)*1000,
                        "error": "sync replica unavailable"}
            # async replicas catch up in background
            for r in self.replicas[1:]:
                threading.Thread(target=r.apply, args=(self.lsn, self.lsn)).start()
        else:
            # async: stream to all replicas in background, return immediately
            for r in self.replicas:
                threading.Thread(target=r.apply, args=(self.lsn, self.lsn)).start()

        return {"ok": True, "latency_ms": (time.time()-t0)*1000,
                "lsn": self.lsn, "mode": self.sync_mode}

def benchmark(primary, n_writes=50):
    lats = []
    for _ in range(n_writes):
        r = primary.write("payload")
        lats.append(r["latency_ms"])
    return lats

if __name__ == "__main__":
    random.seed(42)

    # Setup: 1 primary + 3 replicas (1 sync + 2 async) -- classic HA
    sync_repl  = Replica("sync_repl",  rtt_ms=2)    # same AZ
    async_repl1 = Replica("async_repl1", rtt_ms=20) # cross-AZ
    async_repl2 = Replica("async_repl2", rtt_ms=50) # cross-region

    print("=== Synchronous replication (CP: zero data loss) ===")
    p_sync = Primary("primary", [sync_repl, async_repl1, async_repl2], "sync")
    lats = benchmark(p_sync, n_writes=20)
    print(f"  avg write latency: {sum(lats)/len(lats):.1f}ms")
    print(f"  p99 latency:       {sorted(lats)[-1]:.1f}ms")
    print(f"  data loss on primary crash: 0 (sync replica has every commit)")

    print("\n=== Asynchronous replication (AP: low latency, possible data loss) ===")
    sync_repl2  = Replica("sync_repl",  rtt_ms=2)
    async_repl3 = Replica("async_repl1", rtt_ms=20)
    async_repl4 = Replica("async_repl2", rtt_ms=50)
    p_async = Primary("primary", [sync_repl2, async_repl3, async_repl4], "async")
    lats = benchmark(p_async, n_writes=20)
    print(f"  avg write latency: {sum(lats)/len(lats):.1f}ms")
    print(f"  p99 latency:       {sorted(lats)[-1]:.1f}ms")
    print(f"  data loss on primary crash: up to last few seconds of writes")

    print("\n=== Failure scenario: sync replica goes down ===")
    sync_repl.alive = False
    r = p_sync.write("payload after failure")
    print(f"  sync mode write result: {r}")
    print(f"  -> CP system refuses writes (consistent but unavailable)")

    print("\n=== Failure scenario: sync replica down, async mode ===")
    sync_repl2.alive = False
    r = p_async.write("payload after failure")
    print(f"  async mode write result: ok={r['ok']}, latency={r['latency_ms']:.1f}ms")
    print(f"  -> AP system keeps accepting writes (available but may lose data)")

    print("\n=== Trade-off summary ===")
    print("  SYNC:   + zero data loss, strong consistency")
    print("          - 2x write latency, less available (needs replica quorum)")
    print("  ASYNC:  + low latency, high availability")
    print("          - data loss window (sec), eventual consistency")
    print("  Hybrid: 1 sync replica (durability) + N async replicas (read scale)")
```

quiz.question: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous replication?
options: Replication lag is the time difference between a write committed on the primary and the same write being visible on a replica.
CAP says a distributed system can guarantee at most two of: Consistency (every read sees the latest write), Availability (every request gets a response, no timeouts),…
CouchDB's conflict handler is a JavaScript function.
Synchronous replication means the primary waits for the replica to acknowledge receipt (and usually flush to disk) of the WAL before acknowledging the commit to the client.
quiz.explanation: Synchronous replication means the primary waits for the replica to acknowledge receipt (and usually flush to disk) of the WAL before acknowledging the commit to the client. The client's commit returns only after both the primary and the replica have the data. This gives zero data loss — if the primary crashes immediately after commit, the replica has the data and can be promoted.

options: Replication lag is the time difference between a write committed on the primary and the same write being visible on a replica.

CAP says a distributed system can guarantee at most two of: Consistency (every read sees the latest write), Availability (every request gets a response, no timeouts),…
Use when: write volume fits on one node, you need strong consistency (linearizable writes), and read scaling is the main goal.
quiz.explanation: Single-leader designates one primary that accepts writes; replicas apply the WAL stream. Use when: write volume fits on one node, you need strong consistency (linearizable writes), and read scaling is the main goal. Pros: simple, no write conflicts, easy reasoning.

quiz.question: How does PostgreSQL streaming replication work?
options: Multi-region active-active with multi-leader replication, accepting the conflict resolution cost.
Failover is the process of promoting a replica to primary after the original primary fails.
Synchronous cross-region replication is fundamentally slow because each commit waits for the round-trip to the sync replica.
PostgreSQL streaming replication ships the write-ahead log (WAL) from the primary to replicas over a TCP connection.
quiz.explanation: PostgreSQL streaming replication ships the write-ahead log (WAL) from the primary to replicas over a TCP connection. The primary writes WAL records to pg_wal/ as transactions commit. Replicas connect (via primary_conninfo), request WAL starting from their last-applied position, and the primary streams WAL records as they're generated.

quiz.question: How does MySQL binlog replication differ from PostgreSQL WAL streaming?
options: Multi-region active-active with multi-leader replication, accepting the conflict resolution cost.
Failover is the process of promoting a replica to primary after the original primary fails.
Scale up the primary** — bigger instance with more CPU/RAM/faster disk.
Both ship a log of changes from primary to replica, but the details differ.
quiz.explanation: Both ship a log of changes from primary to replica, but the details differ. MySQL binlog: the primary writes events to a binary log file (binlog); replicas connect via a replication user, fetch binlog events via a "Binlog Dump" thread, write them to a "relay log" on the replica, and apply them via a "SQL thread" (single-threaded in old versions, parallel workers in MySQL 5.7+).

options: CouchDB's conflict handler is a JavaScript function.

quiz.explanation: Replication lag is the time difference between a write committed on the primary and the same write being visible on a replica. With asynchronous replication, lag is non-zero; with synchronous, it's effectively zero (the replica acks before the commit returns). Causes: (1) Network latency — the time to ship WAL from primary to replica.
